vignette: The sirens still wake her before the actual alarm does. At seventy-six, Margaret's body keeps time by the old rhythms. Forty-two years ago, in a city whose name she rarely speaks, the sky splits open. She is a junior fellow on a medical exchange program when the first artillery rounds land. What follows is not a story she tells in pieces. It is a single, heavy thing she carries: the smell of pulverized drywall and diesel, the vibration of concrete stairs under her palms as she crawls toward a basement shelter, the sudden cut of a woman's laughter, the long, quiet hour when the power dies and she presses her forehead against cold stone and waits to see if morning will come. It does. So does the rest. She returns to North America with a suitcase full of textbooks and a nervous system that refuses to power down. When she settles into residency, the darkened reading room of the hospital becomes a refuge. Radiology demands precision. It asks her to look into the body and find what is broken. She learns to trust what she can measure: pixel density, bone margins, the clean line of a rib or the soft cloud of a lung. Her husband, David, meets her in the archives. He knows that her hands will tremble until she finds a patient whose scans are normal, until the world makes geometric sense again. Over the decades, their life grows quiet and deliberate. They keep a house full of books, travel only to places with wide horizons, and never book a flight without checking the weather and the headlines first. Now, in her own clinical space, she still reads the daily load. The PACS screen glows like a window into another body. She notices the way the morning light catches dust on the windowsill and for a fraction of a second, her breath hitches. She tells herself it is only the light. She sits straighter, adjusts her glasses, and focuses on a chest CT. The aorta curves. The pulmonary arteries branch. She writes her report. The work grounds her, but it also keeps her tethered to the old geometry of survival. When the fire alarm tests on Tuesdays, she does not flinch. She simply stops typing, closes her eyes, and counts the spaces between the beeps until they stop. David has learned not to ask what she is remembering during those pauses. He places a mug of tea on the corner of her desk and walks out quietly, knowing she will need a moment before she can speak again. At home, the silence has weight. She sleeps on the side of the bed closest to the door. She leaves the television on a news channel just long enough to scan the map, then clicks it off. She watches the ceiling fan turn and counts its revolutions. Sometimes, when the wind picks up and rattles the gutters, she finds herself pressing her palms flat against the kitchen counter, feeling for the solid line of the house's foundation, as if checking whether the earth is still holding. She does not cry about the past. She simply lives inside the aftermath. Her husband holds her hand at dinner, and she squeezes back, present but distant, like a radio tuned just off the station. The images she reads every day are clear. Her own mind, however, remains a landscape of fog and sudden, bright fractures.
